title: Afsharid and Zand Iran
subtitle: 1722–1789 · Nader Shah's Conquests to Karim Khan's Shiraz

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Afghan occupation, Nader Shah's meteoric rise and fall, and Karim Khan's gentler rule

entries.label: Mahmud and Ashraf Hotak — the Afghan Occupation
entries.hint: The Ghilzai Afghan chief Mahmud Hotak, who had toppled the Safavids at Isfahan, and his cousin and successor Ashraf ruled Iran's former capital as foreign occupiers for seven brutal years, never securing genuine control beyond a few core provinces before Nader's rapidly assembled army expelled them entirely.
entries.note: Muhammad Kazim Marvi, Alam-Ara-yi Naderi, on the Afghan occupation of Isfahan.

entries.label: Nader Shah — the Napoleon of Persia
entries.hint: Rising from minor Khorasani tribal origins through sheer military talent, Nader expelled the Afghans, deposed the last nominal Safavid claimant to crown himself shah in 1736, then conquered as far as Delhi before his later reign collapsed into ruinous taxation, paranoid violence against his own family and officers, and his eventual assassination by the men who had once followed him to those victories.
entries.note: Muhammad Kazim Marvi, Alam-Ara-yi Naderi, the principal contemporary chronicle of Nader Shah's reign.

entries.label: Post-Nader Chaos
entries.hint: Nader's assassination triggered four years of rapid, violent succession disputes among rival claimants and regional strongmen before Karim Khan Zand emerged as the dominant figure in the country's western and central provinces — a brief chaotic interval typical of how quickly a personalist military empire could unravel once its founder was gone.
entries.note: Comparative Iranian chronicle sources on the succession crisis following Nader Shah's death.

entries.label: Karim Khan Zand — the Vakil
entries.hint: Karim Khan governed from Shiraz for nearly three decades under the deliberately modest title Vakil (regent or representative) rather than shah, out of respect for the by-then entirely symbolic Safavid line — a comparatively benevolent and stable reign later Iranian memory would contrast favourably with both Nader's violence before him and the succession chaos that followed his death.
entries.note: Comparative Zand-era chronicle sources; John Perry, Karim Khan Zand (1979).

entries.label: The Zand Succession Crisis
entries.hint: Karim Khan's death set off a decade of fratricidal Zand succession disputes that steadily weakened the dynasty's hold on the country, opening the way for Agha Mohammad Khan of the rival Qajar tribe to begin the brutal reunification campaign that would, within a few years of this folio's close, found Iran's next ruling dynasty.
entries.note: Comparative late Zand-era chronicle sources on the succession disputes of the 1780s.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Expelling the Afghans, the sack of Delhi, and a shah's assassination

entries.label: The Battle of Damghan
entries.hint: Nader's newly assembled army decisively defeated Ashraf Hotak's Afghan forces at Damghan, opening the road to Isfahan and effectively ending seven years of Afghan occupation of the former Safavid capital within a single campaigning season.
entries.note: Muhammad Kazim Marvi, Alam-Ara-yi Naderi, on the Battle of Damghan.

entries.label: The Ottoman Wars
entries.hint: Nader fought recurring campaigns against the Ottoman Empire over the contested Iraqi and Caucasus frontier throughout his reign, including his unsuccessful attempt to have Twelver Shiism recognised as a legitimate fifth school of Sunni jurisprudence as part of a broader peace settlement.
entries.note: Ottoman and Persian chronicle traditions on the recurring Ottoman-Afsharid wars.

entries.label: Nader's Invasion of India and the Sack of Delhi
entries.hint: Nader's army crushed Mughal forces at Karnal and occupied Delhi, where a massacre of the city's population following a riot was followed by the systematic looting of the Mughal treasury — including the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond — plunder so vast that Nader reportedly suspended Iranian taxation for three years upon his return.
entries.note: Muhammad Kazim Marvi, Alam-Ara-yi Naderi; Mughal court chronicle accounts of the Delhi massacre and sack.

entries.label: The Assassination of Nader Shah
entries.hint: A group of his own officers, no longer willing to tolerate his escalating paranoia, brutal taxation and violence against his own family and retinue, assassinated Nader in his camp — the abrupt end of a reign that had briefly made Iran one of the most militarily formidable states in Asia.
entries.note: Muhammad Kazim Marvi, Alam-Ara-yi Naderi, on the circumstances of Nader Shah's assassination.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Nader's ruinous war taxation against Karim Khan's more lenient administration

entries.label: Nader's Ruinous War Taxation
entries.hint: To fund an army kept permanently on campaign, Nader's later reign imposed tax levels contemporary observers described as genuinely ruinous to the ordinary population, extracted with escalating brutality — a fiscal policy that historians identify as a direct cause of the unrest and elite disaffection that culminated in his assassination.
entries.note: Muhammad Kazim Marvi, Alam-Ara-yi Naderi, on the burden of Nader's later-reign taxation.

entries.label: Karim Khan's Lenient Administration
entries.hint: Karim Khan's government pursued deliberately moderate taxation and investment in provincial reconstruction after decades of war damage, an administrative style broadly credited — alongside his own personal reputation for approachability — with the relative peace and modest prosperity his core territories enjoyed during his reign.
entries.note: John Perry, Karim Khan Zand (1979), on Zand-era administrative policy.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Nader's attempt to reconcile Sunni and Shia Islam for political ends

entries.label: Nader's Attempt at Sunni-Shia Reconciliation
entries.hint: Nader convened a conference of Sunni and Shia scholars at Najaf proposing that Twelver Shiism be recognised as a legitimate fifth school (the Ja'fari madhhab) of Sunni jurisprudence rather than a separate heterodox tradition — a political attempt to ease relations with the Sunni Ottoman Empire that gained little lasting traction with either side's religious establishment.
entries.note: Ottoman and Persian diplomatic correspondence on the Najaf conference proposal.

entries.label: Shia Religious Life under the Zands
entries.hint: Karim Khan's reign saw a return to more conventional Safavid-style royal patronage of Twelver Shia institutions after Nader's ecumenical experiments — a quieter, less ideologically ambitious religious policy that matched the generally lower-key character of Zand rule as a whole.
entries.note: Comparative Zand-era religious patronage evidence, Shiraz.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Karim Khan's Shiraz and the looted Peacock Throne

entries.label: The Peacock Throne as Plunder
entries.hint: Nader's seizure of the jewel-encrusted Mughal Peacock Throne, along with the Koh-i-Noor and Darya-ye Noor diamonds, transferred one of the most fabled royal treasures in the world from Delhi to Iran — the throne itself was later broken up, but the diamonds' subsequent journeys through Iranian, and eventually other, royal treasuries kept the legend of the 1739 sack alive for centuries.
entries.note: Contemporary Mughal and Persian court accounts of the Delhi plunder's most celebrated items.

entries.label: Karim Khan's Shiraz
entries.hint: Karim Khan rebuilt Shiraz as his capital with a citadel (the Arg), a congregational mosque, and the Vakil Bazaar — a covered market whose scale and vaulted brickwork construction made it one of the era's most substantial commercial building projects anywhere in Iran, reflecting the relative peace and modest prosperity of his reign.
entries.note: Arg of Karim Khan and Vakil Bazaar, Shiraz, extant structures.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Court chroniclers assess two very different kinds of ruler

entries.label: Marvi's Chronicle of Nader Shah
entries.hint: Muhammad Kazim Marvi's Alam-Ara-yi Naderi provides the essential contemporary narrative of Nader Shah's entire career, written by an author with direct access to court circles — the source against which nearly every modern account of Nader's rise, conquests and final descent into tyranny is still checked.
entries.note: Muhammad Kazim Marvi, Alam-Ara-yi Naderi.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: A population impoverished by decades of war, then a brief recovery

entries.label: Decades of War Impoverish the Population
entries.hint: Between the Afghan occupation, Nader's near-constant campaigning and his punishing wartime taxation, Iran's population and agricultural economy suffered a documented and severe decline across this period — a demographic and economic low point from which recovery only began in earnest under the comparative stability of Karim Khan's later reign.
entries.note: Comparative demographic and economic history of 18th-century Iran; contemporary European merchant reports on wartime economic conditions.

entries.label: Modest Recovery under Karim Khan
entries.hint: Karim Khan actively encouraged the revival of trade through Shiraz and the southern port of Bushehr, including renewed contact with the English East India Company — a deliberate policy of commercial reconstruction that made his reign's relative prosperity as much a matter of active economic policy as simply the absence of Nader's wars.
entries.note: English East India Company factory records on renewed trade under Karim Khan.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Continuity beneath an interlude of war and reconstruction

entries.label: Nader's Artillery Reforms
entries.hint: Nader invested significantly in modernising Persian artillery and firearms production, a direct response to the same gunpowder-technology gap that had hurt Safavid forces at Chaldiran two centuries earlier — military modernisation that contributed materially to his run of battlefield successes against both Ottoman and Mughal forces.
entries.note: Comparative military-technological analysis of Afsharid-era Persian artillery development.

entries.label: The Vakil Bazaar's Vaulted Construction
entries.hint: The Vakil Bazaar's long vaulted brick corridors, built to a scale supporting a major revival of Shiraz's commercial life, represent a return to substantial civic construction after decades in which building activity across most of Iran had been a low priority for war-focused rulers.
entries.note: Vakil Bazaar, Shiraz, extant structure.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Diplomacy with the Ottomans, the Mughals and Russia

entries.label: Nader's Diplomacy with Russia and the Ottomans
entries.hint: Nader conducted active diplomacy alongside his wars, negotiating the return of Caspian territory from Russia (occupied since the chaos of the Afghan period) and repeated peace settlements with the Ottomans — a ruler who used negotiation and conquest as complementary tools rather than relying on military force alone.
entries.note: Russian and Ottoman diplomatic correspondence with the Afsharid court.

entries.label: Karim Khan's Trade Agreement with the East India Company
entries.hint: Karim Khan granted the English East India Company trading privileges at Bushehr, part of a deliberate policy of encouraging renewed European commercial contact with southern Iran after decades in which war had disrupted most established trade relationships.
entries.note: English East India Company records on the 1763 Bushehr trade agreement.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A conqueror who helped hasten the Mughal Empire's own decline

entries.label: Nader's Campaigns Hasten Mughal Decline
entries.hint: The Mughal Empire never recovered the prestige or central authority it lost when Nader's army sacked Delhi in 1739 — the invasion accelerated a fragmentation into effectively independent regional successor states that, decades later, the expanding British East India Company would exploit province by province.
entries.note: Comparative Mughal political history following the 1739 Persian invasion and sack of Delhi.

entries.label: A Brief Return to Great-Power Status, Then Relapse
entries.hint: For roughly a decade under Nader, Iran was arguably the most militarily formidable state between the Ottoman Empire and Mughal India — a position that evaporated almost as quickly as it had appeared, leaving a fragmented, comparatively modest Zand state that never attempted to reclaim Nader's conquests beyond Iran's own historic frontiers.
entries.note: Comparative regional power assessment of Afsharid Iran at its territorial peak versus the subsequent Zand period.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The human cost of Nader's wars, and Karim Khan's contrasting reputation

entries.label: The Human Cost of Nader's Wars
entries.hint: Beyond the fiscal burden, Nader's later campaigns relied on increasingly coercive military conscription and forced labour drawn from a population already exhausted by decades of war — the human toll of his conquests fell overwhelmingly on ordinary villagers and townspeople who saw none of the plunder his armies brought home from Delhi.
entries.note: Muhammad Kazim Marvi, Alam-Ara-yi Naderi, on conscription and popular hardship under Nader's later reign.

entries.label: Karim Khan's Reputation for Accessibility
entries.hint: Persian popular tradition remembers Karim Khan as personally accessible to ordinary petitioners and notably averse to the ceremonial remoteness other Iranian rulers cultivated — whether or not every anecdote is literally accurate, the consistency of this reputation across independent sources suggests a genuinely different relationship between ruler and ruled than either Nader's reign or the preceding Safavid court had offered.
entries.note: Comparative Zand-era popular and chronicle traditions regarding Karim Khan's personal conduct.
